audits.title: Assessing the compliance of accurately documenting medication history in CAMHS – completion of the audit cycle
audits.standard: Locally agreed protocol: medication history recorded in specified section of PARIS database
audits.setting: Seven CAMHS teams, south Derbyshire, Derbyshire Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust

cycle1.result: 13% had medication recorded in the correct section of PARIS

audits.intervention: Teaching for teams following the 2017 audit

cycle2.result: 58/78 (74%) recorded in correct section; of those, 86% drug names correct, 79% correct dose, 71% correct frequency, 81% regular/PRN recorded

audits.other_findings: Compliance varied between teams from 0% to 100%. Further teaching delivered and move to System One supported.
audits.citation: Guest L, Mudiyanselage I, Ambekar S, Lankappa S. Assessing the compliance of accurately documenting medication history in CAMHS – completion of the audit cycle. BJPsych Open. 2021;7(Suppl 1):S27-S27.

audits.title: Audit: Do Electronic Mental Health Records Match General Practice Shared Records of Medications and Allergies for Patients Residing at a Community Forensic Supported Accommodation?
audits.standard: Trust medicines reconciliation guidance: 100% concordance between mental health and general practice records for medication and allergies
audits.setting: Community forensic supported accommodation, Cumbria, Northumberland, Tyne and Wear NHS Foundation Trust

cycle1.result: Allergy status discrepancy in 2 patients (25%); medication discrepancy in 2 patients (25%), both vitamin D omitted from mental health records

audits.other_findings: Allergies were documented in ward discharge summaries but not in GP records; primary care asked to update. Re-audits every four months planned.
audits.citation: Bernard K, Sud N. Audit: Do Electronic Mental Health Records Match General Practice Shared Records of Medications and Allergies for Patients Residing at a Community Forensic Supported Accommodation?. BJPsych Open. 2022;8(Suppl 1):S177-S178.

audits.title: Enhancing Patient Safety: Audit of Medicines Reconciliation of Psychiatry Inpatients in NHS Lanarkshire 2023–24
audits.standard: Scottish Patient Safety Programme and NICE: 95% of medicines reconciled within 24 hours of admission; local medicines reconciliation guidelines
audits.setting: General adult psychiatry wards 19 and 20, University Hospital Hairmyres, NHS Lanarkshire

cycle1.result: 70% of forms completed within 24 hours; two sources of information used in 66%

audits.intervention: Summary document of latest guidelines and link to an e-learning module distributed to resident doctors and raised at monthly resident doctors' meeting

cycle2.result: 100% of forms completed within 24 hours; two sources used in 100%; improvement in all 12 areas assessed

audits.other_findings: Results may reflect individual variability between clerking doctors.
audits.citation: Iyer A. Enhancing Patient Safety: Audit of Medicines Reconciliation of Psychiatry Inpatients in NHS Lanarkshire 2023–24. BJPsych Open. 2025;11(S1):S245-S246. doi:10.1192/bjo.2025.10609.

audits.title: An initial audit – a step in the journey to improve admission medication reconciliation compliance and accuracy for admitted psychiatric patients
audits.standard: Medication reconciliation as a WHO safety initiative (Accreditation Canada ROP 2020 handbook): documented BPMH with ≥2 information sources

cycle1.result: 21/22 (95%) had a documented admission BPMH; 15/21 (71%) had at least one discrepancy, mostly omissions (10/17, 59%); ≥2 information sources documented in 1/21 (4.8%).

audits.intervention: Findings shared with clinicians; DIS MedRec form with pre-populated provincial Drug Information System medication list implemented in late September 2025, with staff education.
audits.other_findings: Pre- and post-intervention data collection (June–August 2025 vs November 2025–January 2026) is ongoing.
audits.citation: Raji A, Crowdis J, Asurappulige G, Singh S, Sharma A, Ali J, et al.. An initial audit – a step in the journey to improve admission medication reconciliation compliance and accuracy for admitted psychiatric patients. European Psychiatry. 2026;69(S1):S923-S923. doi:10.1192/j.eurpsy.2026.11711.

audits.title: Implementing online medication reconciliation at a large academic medical center.
audits.standard: Completion of admission and discharge medication reconciliation
audits.setting: Bellevue Hospital, New York City, large academic medical centre
audits.intervention: Online medication reconciliation made mandatory at admission with an EHR blocking function (April 2007), then mandatory discharge reconciliation (November 2007).
audits.other_findings: An earlier paper-based pilot in 2005 was unsuccessful.
audits.citation: Bails D, Clayton K, Roy K, Cantor MN. Implementing online medication reconciliation at a large academic medical center. Jt Comm J Qual Patient Saf. 2008;34(9):499-508. doi:10.1016/s1553-7250(08)34063-x. PMID: 18792654.

audits.title: Medicines Reconciliation on Admission to Inpatient Psychiatric Care: Findings from a UK Quality Improvement Programme.
audits.standard: Two or more sources of information consulted about current medicines (proxy for medicines reconciliation)

cycle1.result: Medicines reconciliation possible in 71%; discrepancies found in 25% of these.

cycle2.result: Medicines reconciliation possible in 79%; discrepancies found in 31%.

audits.other_findings: Task was most often done by pharmacy staff within 24 hours of admission.

audits.title: Applying quality improvement methods to address gaps in medicines reconciliation at transfers of care from an acute UK hospital.
audits.standard: Reliable documentation of current medication on discharge summaries (complete, verified, intentional changes clarified)
audits.setting: Acute admissions unit, Chelsea and Westminster Hospital, 400-bed teaching hospital, London

cycle1.result: Reliable documentation of current medication on 49.2% of discharge summaries during the project (10 random patients per week).

audits.intervention: Staff education and training, medication documentation templates for electronic prescribing and discharge summaries co-designed with patients, and pharmacist-led team approach.

cycle2.result: Reliable documentation 85.2% in a post-study audit.

audits.other_findings: Pharmacist involvement in discharge reconciliation increased; variation seen at doctor changeover and introduction of new systems.
audits.citation: Marvin V, Kuo S, Poots AJ, Woodcock T, Vaughan L, Bell D. Applying quality improvement methods to address gaps in medicines reconciliation at transfers of care from an acute UK hospital. BMJ Open. 2016;6(6):e010230. doi:10.1136/bmjopen-2015-010230. PMID: 27288369.

audits.title: Addressing prescription discrepancies in renal patients: a prospective audit.
audits.standard: Hospital medication record matches current prescription (patients bring a medication list)
audits.setting: Renal outpatient clinics, Royal Bournemouth Hospital

cycle1.result: Median proportion failing to bring a list or recall medications 0.45; significant discrepancies in 10.9% of those forgetting a list.

cycle2.result: Median proportion 0.30 (0.36 in 2015; Chi-sq = 46.94, p < 0.001); significant discrepancies fell to 3.9%.

audits.citation: Lam S, Docherty S, Taylor JE. Addressing prescription discrepancies in renal patients: a prospective audit. J R Coll Physicians Edinb. 2018;48(1):16-19. doi:10.4997/jrcpe.2018.103. PMID: 29741519.

audits.title: Please reconcile, not wait a while.
audits.standard: 100% of paediatric patients to have regular medications prescribed by mid-day the day after admission
audits.setting: Paediatric ward, The Hillingdon Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust (district general hospital)

cycle1.result: Baseline medicines reconciliation by doctors accurately completed 50% of the time; mean rate during PDSA cycles 79%.

audits.intervention: Teaching sessions for doctors, awareness posters and questionnaires for parents/children about regular medications (PDSA cycles).
audits.other_findings: About 40 patients reviewed per week; 100% achieved on 34 occasions and continuously for the last 3 weeks.
audits.citation: Trivedi A, Sharma S, Ajitsaria R, Davey NJ. Please reconcile, not wait a while. Arch Dis Child Educ Pract Ed. 2020;105(2):122-126. doi:10.1136/archdischild-2018-316356. PMID: 31073034.

audits.title: Evaluation of a Novel Audit Tool for Medication Reconciliation at Hospital Discharge.
audits.standard: Discharge medication reconciliation quality audit tool (Canadian Patient Safety Institute and ISMP Canada), modified
audits.setting: General internal medicine services at 3 academic hospitals (McMaster University, Hamilton, Ontario)

cycle1.result: Documentation of any discharge medication reconciliation for only 1 patient (3%); none carried out by pharmacists.

audits.other_findings: Post-discharge interviews showed major communication gaps with community pharmacists and family physicians.

audits.title: Are we meeting current standards in medicines reconciliation? A study in a District General Hospital.
audits.standard: NICE and Scottish Patient Safety Programme: 95% of patients to have medicines reconciliation within 24 hours of admission
audits.setting: Acute surgical receiving ward, Hairmyres Hospital, NHS Lanarkshire, district general hospital

cycle1.result: 46% reconciled on admission and 77% within 24 hours (abstract states 49% and 75%)

audits.intervention: Emergency Care Summary access for junior doctors plus lunchtime teaching and email reinforcement

cycle2.result: Third cycle: 57% completed on admission and 84% at 24 hours; 89% had a complete medication history

audits.other_findings: Second cycle showed 62% on admission and 86% at 24 hours with 93% accurate history; performance slipped at the third cycle and never reached 95%. Six patients were lost to follow up and three discharged within 24 hours at baseline.
audits.citation: Iddles E, Williamson A, Bradley A, Khan K. Are we meeting current standards in medicines reconciliation? A study in a District General Hospital. BMJ Qual Improv Rep. 2015;4(1):u207508.w3002. doi:10.1136/bmjquality.u207508.w3002. PMID: 26734398.
